details:
ROBI is a health monitoring system for astronauts on long-duration missions, where crews must notice their own health changes without a doctor on board. Its software, also called ROBI, runs on the spacecraft computer. It collects eight indicators (resting heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose from a continuous patch, body temperature, sleep, mood, radiation exposure and bone health), compares each reading with the astronaut’s personal baseline, and shows a color-coded status: green, yellow, orange or red. A single abnormal value creates a note. A sustained trend creates an alert with a clear next step, including contacting the flight surgeon on the ground. The software never diagnoses; it guides the astronaut.

The physical interface is a small 3D-printable robot. The astronaut talks to it, places a finger or arm against its sensors, and the robot sends time-stamped readings to the software. The planned hardware includes an ESP32-class controller, a pulse sensor, an infrared thermal sensor, a blood pressure cuff with a pump, a camera for facial expressions, an RGB LED ring for emotion colors, a speaker and a reader for the glucose patch. The current prototype is a web app with simulated data and a printable 3D model sized for a Bambu Lab A1 mini.

The benefits are early detection of small changes, clear actions, and support for well-being through guided breathing, mood check-ins, creative writing and personalized exercise. The intended impact is safer long missions, with astronauts who understand their own data and can share a concise summary with ground teams.

We built the prototype with HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, and used Canva for the presentation. We used AI assistance to help write and build the prototype, as disclosed in the SI section.

The concept is creative because the robot gives the health data a friendly face. The ROBI idea began as a 2025 class project, and it now combines emotional support with physical measurements. The team considered astronaut autonomy, offline operation, privacy (encrypted storage, strict access and anonymized research data), and low workload during demanding tasks. All reference ranges are illustrative and must be validated with a medical advisor before any real use.
